title: Price Your Distribution Power Honestly
documentTitle: Apple EMG Deal Review — Google Search Partnership Presentation (June 4, 2007)
excerptForBlog:
Deal Overview

• Current deal terms: Google default (and exclusive) search provider in Safari browser; 50% Net Revenue Share after 10% deductions for queries stemming from the Apple browser chrome; term through January 2008.

• What Apple wants: Launching Safari for PCs and wants current deal terms to apply to this new OS; Google to be one of two possible choices for search provider (not default), with user required to choose search provider prior to using browser; Apple wants current deal terms to extend to Safari browser for PC OS; contract open re: OS, but requires Google to be the default search provider to qualify for revenue share.

• Key issues: Apple uncooperative vis-à-vis Google's efforts on Chrome utilizing their open source platform; strategic considerations with respect to supporting PC version of Safari vis-à-vis Chrome launch plans; revenue share seems rich for non-default and non-exclusive deal.

Impact if Existing Deal Terms

• Likely Scenario: Assume new browser has same chrome query growth as Firefox had in its first year; apply the rev share we give Safari (45% of gross); annual rev share payment to Apple would = $90M.

• Aggressive Scenario: Assume new browser comes out of the gate with the same worldwide market share as Firefox (20%); annual rev share payment to Apple would = $205M.

pullQuote: When a partner asks for the same price on a worse deal, the right answer starts with naming what you're actually buying.
leadershipTraits: prices deals in dollars, not adjectives
tracks partner behavior across the whole relationship
willing to push back on a powerful counterparty
situation: In June 2007, Google executive Jeff Shardell wrote an internal deal review analyzing Apple's request to extend their existing Safari search partnership to a new PC version of Safari. The current deal gave Google exclusive default search in Safari for a 45% gross revenue share. Apple's new ask was different: Google would be just one of two user-selectable options, not the default. The internal model put the cost at $90M in a likely scenario and $205M in an aggressive one.
insight: The document flags three tensions at once. First, the economics are broken: the existing revenue share was priced for exclusivity and default placement. Apple was now asking for the same rate without those terms. The memo notes plainly that 'revenue share seems rich for non-default and non-exclusive deal.' Second, there's a platform conflict: Apple was 'uncooperative' with Google's efforts on Chrome using Apple's open-source platform, while Google was preparing its own browser launch. Paying Apple $90–205M per year while Apple blocked Chrome's development would mean funding a competitive obstacle. Third, the memo shows Google thinking in scenarios — not just one number, but a range tied to Firefox's growth trajectory. That's disciplined: anchor the downside, stress-test the upside, then decide. The hidden move here is recognizing that deal terms must reprice when the strategic value changes. Default placement is a different product than optional placement, and the document treats it that way.
application: Before renewing any partnership, list the specific conditions that justified the original terms — exclusivity, default status, platform access, whatever they were. If any condition has changed, reprice before you renegotiate. Never let a partner reframe a lesser arrangement as the same deal.
